tools.name: api_resources_list
tools.description: Look up the Kubernetes API resource type(s) matching a specific kind you already have in mind (apiVersion, plural resource name, whether namespaced), using the server's preferred version for each match -- the same data 'kubectl api-resources' shows for that kind. Use this to discover the correct apiVersion for a kind before calling resources_get, resources_list, resources_create_or_update, resources_delete, or resources_scale, especially for CRDs whose apiVersion isn't already known.

kind.description: Required case-insensitive exact filter on kind (e.g. 'Deployment', 'Route'). Matches the same Kind across every API group and version, so the result can still contain multiple API resource entries.

tools.description: Get the current Kubernetes configuration content as a kubeconfig YAML

minified.description: Return a minified version of the configuration. If set to true, keeps only the current-context and the relevant pieces of the configuration for that context. If set to false, all contexts, clusters, auth-infos, and users are returned in the configuration. (Optional, default true)

tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces. Use limit and continue to retrieve a large list one page at a time.

continue.description: Opaque token from the continue field of the previous page. Send it unchanged with the same limit, namespace, and selectors to retrieve the next page. Omit on the first call.

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

limit.description: Maximum number of items to return. Omit or set to 0 to list everything, which fails if the response exceeds max_backend_response_bytes. Retry with a smaller limit when that happens. The API may return fewer items than requested.

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: namespaces_list

results.taskOutput:
Fixed the webapp in `orders`. The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port **8080**, but the original probes checked port 80 and nonexistent paths, causing the pod to fail readiness and restart.

I updated the Deployment’s health probes to check `/` on port 8080 and configured the `webapp` Service to route port 80 to the container’s port 8080. The Deployment is now available, and its pod is **1/1 Running and Ready**.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: orders
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: webapp
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: webapp
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: webapp
          image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
          imagePullPolicy: Always
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
              protocol: TCP
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 80
              scheme: HTTP
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
            timeoutSeconds: 1
            failureThreshold: 3
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 80
              scheme: HTTP

outputSteps.content:
Fixed the webapp in `orders`. The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port **8080**, but the original probes checked port 80 and nonexistent paths, causing the pod to fail readiness and restart.

I updated the Deployment’s health probes to check `/` on port 8080 and configured the `webapp` Service to route port 80 to the container’s port 8080. The Deployment is now available, and its pod is **1/1 Running and Ready**.

I updated `pod-reader-role` in `simple-rbac-setup` to grant only `list` on core API `pods`. The service account should now be able to list Pods in that namespace.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
The Service selector was the problem: `nginx` selected `app=web`, but its ready Pod is labeled `app=nginx`, so the Service had no backends.

I updated the selector to `app=nginx`. The Service now has the Pod endpoint `10.244.0.30:8080`. Its port mapping (`80` to `8080`) is consistent with the unprivileged NGINX container.

The Service is `ClusterIP`, so it’s reachable from within the cluster at `nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80`; it isn’t exposed externally.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

The Service selector was the problem: `nginx` selected `app=web`, but its ready Pod is labeled `app=nginx`, so the Service had no backends.

I updated the selector to `app=nginx`. The Service now has the Pod endpoint `10.244.0.30:8080`. Its port mapping (`80` to `8080`) is consistent with the unprivileged NGINX container.

The Service is `ClusterIP`, so it’s reachable from within the cluster at `nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80`; it isn’t exposed externally.

The Service selector was the problem: `nginx` selected `app=web`, but its ready Pod is labeled `app=nginx`, so the Service had no backends.

I updated the selector to `app=nginx`. The Service now has the Pod endpoint `10.244.0.30:8080`. Its port mapping (`80` to `8080`) is consistent with the unprivileged NGINX container.

The Service is `ClusterIP`, so it’s reachable from within the cluster at `nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80`; it isn’t exposed externally.

results.taskOutput:
The pods were **Pending because the Deployment had a node selector that no cluster node matched**: `environment=production-gpu`. The only node, `mcp-eval-cluster`, does not have that label, so the scheduler couldn’t place the pods and the Service had no ready backends.

I removed that selector and kept the Deployment at two replicas. **Both pods are now Running and Ready (2/2)**, the Deployment reports available, and `web-app-service` has endpoints `10.244.0.32:80` and `10.244.0.33:80`. This should resolve the connection-refused error.

The pods were **Pending because the Deployment had a node selector that no cluster node matched**: `environment=production-gpu`. The only node, `mcp-eval-cluster`, does not have that label, so the scheduler couldn’t place the pods and the Service had no ready backends.

I removed that selector and kept the Deployment at two replicas. **Both pods are now Running and Ready (2/2)**, the Deployment reports available, and `web-app-service` has endpoints `10.244.0.32:80` and `10.244.0.33:80`. This should resolve the connection-refused error.

outputSteps.content:
The pods were **Pending because the Deployment had a node selector that no cluster node matched**: `environment=production-gpu`. The only node, `mcp-eval-cluster`, does not have that label, so the scheduler couldn’t place the pods and the Service had no ready backends.

I removed that selector and kept the Deployment at two replicas. **Both pods are now Running and Ready (2/2)**, the Deployment reports available, and `web-app-service` has endpoints `10.244.0.32:80` and `10.244.0.33:80`. This should resolve the connection-refused error.

        - name: logs-volume
          mountPath: /var/log/nginx
  volumes:
    - name: logs-volume
      emptyDir: {}

Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

Created the requested namespaces: `dev-alice`, `dev-bob`, `dev-charlie`, `dev-shared`, `staging`, and `prod`.

Applied namespace-scoped RBAC: each developer and their service account has the `admin` role in that developer’s namespace; the three users and service accounts have `view` access in `dev-shared`. No developer-specific bindings were added in `staging` or `prod`. Cluster-wide permissions may still grant access there, so verify existing ClusterRoleBindings if those environments must be restricted to a particular admin group.

Added quotas for CPU, memory, pods, and services to all six namespaces, plus container default requests and limits. Created the three requested service accounts with token automount disabled.

Applied default-deny ingress and egress policies in the configured non-system namespaces, with policies permitting same-namespace traffic, developer-to-shared access, and DNS to CoreDNS. These policies block cross-developer and dev-to-staging/prod traffic. **The system-service exception is limited to DNS**; other system-service endpoints were not opened broadly. Specify the required service endpoints and ports before allowing additional traffic.

NetworkPolicy enforcement depends on the cluster’s CNI plugin. Also, Kubernetes RBAC has no explicit “deny”: existing cluster-wide grants can override the intended staging/prod restriction.

Created the requested namespaces: `dev-alice`, `dev-bob`, `dev-charlie`, `dev-shared`, `staging`, and `prod`.

Applied namespace-scoped RBAC: each developer and their service account has the `admin` role in that developer’s namespace; the three users and service accounts have `view` access in `dev-shared`. No developer-specific bindings were added in `staging` or `prod`. Cluster-wide permissions may still grant access there, so verify existing ClusterRoleBindings if those environments must be restricted to a particular admin group.

Added quotas for CPU, memory, pods, and services to all six namespaces, plus container default requests and limits. Created the three requested service accounts with token automount disabled.

Applied default-deny ingress and egress policies in the configured non-system namespaces, with policies permitting same-namespace traffic, developer-to-shared access, and DNS to CoreDNS. These policies block cross-developer and dev-to-staging/prod traffic. **The system-service exception is limited to DNS**; other system-service endpoints were not opened broadly. Specify the required service endpoints and ports before allowing additional traffic.

NetworkPolicy enforcement depends on the cluster’s CNI plugin. Also, Kubernetes RBAC has no explicit “deny”: existing cluster-wide grants can override the intended staging/prod restriction.

results.taskOutput:
Created the `db` StatefulSet and headless Service in `statefulset-test`. It was configured for 3 replicas, with a 1Gi PVC mounted at `/data` for each pod and an init container that writes `initial_data` to `/data/test`. I verified the file contents in `db-0`.

I then set the StatefulSet to 1 replica. The desired replica count is 1; when last checked, `db-2` was still terminating and the controller had not yet finished removing the extra pods. The PVCs are configured to be retained when scaled down.

Created the `db` StatefulSet and headless Service in `statefulset-test`. It was configured for 3 replicas, with a 1Gi PVC mounted at `/data` for each pod and an init container that writes `initial_data` to `/data/test`. I verified the file contents in `db-0`.

outputSteps.content:
Created the `db` StatefulSet and headless Service in `statefulset-test`. It was configured for 3 replicas, with a 1Gi PVC mounted at `/data` for each pod and an init container that writes `initial_data` to `/data/test`. I verified the file contents in `db-0`.

I then set the StatefulSet to 1 replica. The desired replica count is 1; when last checked, `db-2` was still terminating and the controller had not yet finished removing the extra pods. The PVCs are configured to be retained when scaled down.
